title: Building Bridges with the Area Model: From Multiplication to Algebra
author: Jon Fant
summary: Jon Fant argues that many maths curricula inadvertently teach multiplication as a sequence of eight or more disconnected methods - from early counting through to factorising double brackets - when a single coherent representation, the area model, could carry students through the entire journey with a consistent underlying meaning. He traces this journey in detail: starting with arrays connecting multiplication to physical area as early as ages 4-5, using arrays to give students an intuitive, visual grasp of the commutative law, scaling up to times-table squares as scaled area models, and then extending the same area model to multi-digit multiplication by incorporating place value through partitioning (e.g., 54 x 23 as (50+4) x (20+3)). Fant distinguishes this from the traditional 'grid method,' which he says he deliberately stopped using, arguing that framing the grid explicitly as an area model - and highlighting the diagonal place-value structure within it - gives students a deeper conceptual layer rather than just a procedure for arriving at the right answer. He positions the area model as a natural bridge toward more efficient methods like lattice multiplication, and ultimately toward algebraic concepts like expanding brackets, factorisation, and polynomial division, all built on the same underlying visual structure students met at age 4 or 5.
points: Fant's central critique: many students experience multiplication as eight or more disconnected methods across their schooling, from early counting to factorising double brackets, with no unifying representation tying the methods together.

His proposed alternative: the area model, introduced via arrays as early as ages 4-5, can serve as a single continuous representation that scales all the way from basic multiplication to polynomial division and completing the square.

A key conceptual move: arrays give students a visual, intuitive grasp of the commutative law (a 3x4 array occupies the same space as a 4x3 array) well before they encounter the abstract algebraic statement of it.

Fant distinguishes his 'area model' framing from the traditional 'grid method' he says he abandoned - by explicitly connecting the grid to the concept of area and highlighting place value running through its diagonals, students get a deeper conceptual layer rather than a rote procedure.

The area model, structured this way, becomes a natural bridge to more efficient methods like lattice multiplication and later to algebraic operations, since it moves students progressively from concrete manipulatives to increasingly abstract visual representations.
quotes: If you consider multiplication from early multiplication to factorising double brackets, maybe you are teaching 8 different methods of multiplication?
What if we could use one model and then compare and contrast the changes to that model at each point.

This early connection, potentially as early as ages 4 or 5, is crucial. Students can see the different shapes, use different items before building with multilink cubes and counting squares within rectangles.

In my previous post I mentioned how historically I stopped using 'grid method'. A key difference I see is that the rebranding of the area model means that this is not simply a method for students to arrive at the correct answer; it has a deeper, connected layer.
